title: The Whole World Blind
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Writing the morning after the January 6, 2021 assault on the U.S. Capitol, Dave Stuart Jr. sets aside his usual teaching-practice content to process the event with his readers as a fellow 'colleague.' His central claim is that dehumanizing or caricaturing one's political neighbors is a losing strategy regardless of political affiliation, personally corrosive to the soul and socially corrosive to the body politic. He draws on Martin Luther King Jr.'s Strength to Love, particularly King's concept of the 'enemy-neighbor,' to argue that even a person's worst deeds never express the whole of who they are. Charity, in Stuart's reading of King, is not a feeling summoned in a moment or a gesture like a social media post, but a practiced virtue built through small, repeated daily choices, much like humility or honesty. He closes by arguing that educators are uniquely positioned to model this kind of practiced love for a watching world, and invites readers to spend the coming weekend in reflection, prayer, or rest rather than reactive commentary.
points: Writing the day after the January 6, 2021 Capitol riot, Stuart argues that political disdain for one's neighbor is corrosive at both a personal level (it 'weakens the soul') and a social one, regardless of which side holds the disdain.

He leans on Martin Luther King Jr.'s Strength to Love to reframe political opponents as 'enemy-neighbors' whose worst actions never express the whole of who they are, a direct rebuttal to caricaturing groups by their worst members.

Charity, per Stuart, is a practiced virtue rather than a feeling or a single gesture; 'you don't decide in a moment to be charitable' by writing an email or attending a protest, it's built through repetition like any other moral habit.

Stuart explicitly nominates educators as best positioned to model this practiced love to a 'watching world,' framing the classroom relationship itself as a site of moral formation, not just instruction.
quotes: When in our hearts we diminish our neighbors, we lose. Whether you're politically left or right or centrist or agnostic, the disdain of one's neighbor is a cancer to the flourishing life.
It is personally dangerous — it weakens the soul itself — and it is socially dangerous — it weakens society.

We must recognize that the evil deeds of the enemy-neighbor, the thing that hurts, never quite expresses all that he is. An element of goodness may be found even in our worst enemy. Each of us is something of a schizophrenic personality, tragically divided against ourselves.

It's love with muscles and love with a brain — a love experienced not as flighty emotion but as a honed and settled state of the will. Like the other moral virtues — such as humility or honesty or forgiveness — charity is not a thing you get by hoping.
You don't "decide" in a moment to be charitable. You don't write an email or post a meme or attend a protest. You practice charity; you practice love.

I think it unlikely to be some big event that does it. Instead, it's probably a billion small decisions enacted by a hundred million people: small, daily efforts at the practice of a loving, enemy-neighbor-seeking life.

There's not a single better group of people to exemplify such a life of love to a watching world than you and me. Why shouldn't it be educators? We could really be something if we loved like that, couldn't we?
